title: FastAPI: background jobs, Celery, health checks and secrets
description: FastAPI BackgroundTasks, Celery retries and beat schedules, duplicate runs across workers, Redis locks, health probes and secrets handling with pydantic.
source: FastAPI documentation (BackgroundTasks); Celery documentation (tasks, retrying, beat, acks_late); APScheduler documentation; redis-py documentation; Kubernetes probe documentation; pydantic-settings documentation
seriesDescription: FastAPI structure and Depends, routing and Pydantic validation, error handling, middleware, async, API design, jobs and health. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: FastAPI `BackgroundTasks` run after the response has been sent.
questions.reason: `BackgroundTasks` run in the same process as the web server, so they are lost if that process dies.

whys.a: Wrong: where they run does not explain when they run.
whys.b: Correct: both are true, but R is a separate durability limitation, not the reason for the timing.

questions.explanation: Good for small jobs like e-mails. For retries, durability or heavy CPU work use Celery, RQ, Arq or a queue.

questions.prompt: Write a FastAPI `POST /signup` handler `signup(email: str, tasks: BackgroundTasks)` that queues `send_welcome_email(email)` to run after the response and answers with status code 202.
questions.explanation: The task function and args are passed separately to `add_task`. Both async and plain functions are accepted.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: A job added with FastAPI `BackgroundTasks` survives a restart of the server process.
questions.reason: `BackgroundTasks` run inside the same process as the web server.

whys.c: Wrong: A is false; R is true.
whys.d: Correct: because the work lives only in that process, a restart or crash drops unfinished jobs. R is true and is the reason A is false.

questions.explanation: Use a durable queue (Celery, RQ, Arq, a database outbox) when the job must survive restarts or needs retries.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Celery tasks should be written to be idempotent.
questions.reason: Celery guarantees exactly-once execution by default.

whys.c: Correct: A is true, R is false; delivery is at-least-once, especially with acks_late or visibility timeouts.

questions.explanation: Redelivery after a worker crash or timeout can run a task twice, so use idempotency keys or upserts.

questions.prompt: Write a Celery task `send_email(self, to)` bound to itself (`bind=True`), allowing at most 3 retries with a 10 second default delay. It calls `deliver(to)` and, if that raises `ConnectionError`, retries the task with the caught exception.
questions.explanation: Verified with an eager Celery app: a task that always fails runs 4 times (the first call plus 3 retries). Raising `self.retry` (rather than just calling it) ends the current run immediately.
questions.starter:
from celery import Celery
celery = Celery("jobs")

questions.prompt: A Celery task declared with `max_retries=3` always fails and calls `self.retry(exc=exc)` each time. It is published once. How many times does the task body run in total?
questions.explanation: One initial run plus 3 retries gives 4 executions (verified by running an eager Celery app). After the last retry the original exception is raised.

questions.prompt: Write a Celery beat schedule on `celery.conf` that runs the task `"tasks.cleanup"` every day at 02:00 using `crontab`, under the entry name `"nightly-cleanup"`.
questions.explanation: Run exactly one beat process; two beats would enqueue every job twice. Workers then execute the tasks, and the task itself should still be idempotent.

questions.prompt: A FastAPI service starts an in-process `APScheduler` with a nightly cron job inside its `lifespan` handler. It is deployed with 4 `uvicorn` worker processes on each of 2 machines. How many times does the job fire each night across the whole deployment?
questions.explanation: Each worker process runs its own `lifespan` and therefore its own scheduler: 4 x 2 = 8 runs. Run the scheduler in one dedicated process, use a distributed lock, or move scheduling to Celery beat or a cluster cron job.

questions.prompt: Python with `redis-py`: at the start of a scheduled job, take a lock so only one instance runs it. Use the single atomic call that sets key `lock:nightly` only if it does not exist, expiring after 300 seconds, and return early if the lock was not acquired.

checks.label: sets a TTL with ex= (or px=)
returns when the lock was not acquired

questions.explanation: `SET NX EX` is atomic, unlike `SETNX` followed by `EXPIRE`. Pick a TTL longer than the job, or renew it. A lock library such as `redis-py`'s `Lock` adds renewal and ownership checks.

questions.prompt: Write `GET /health/ready` for FastAPI. Call `db_ping()` (raises on failure); on success return `{"status": "ok"}`, on failure answer HTTP 503.
questions.explanation: A `JSONResponse(status_code=503)` is equally fine. Keep readiness cheap and time-boxed.

questions.prompt: A FastAPI service depends on PostgreSQL and runs under Kubernetes. Where should the database ping live so that a database outage does not cause a restart storm?

options.text: In `/health/live`, so pods that lose the database are restarted quickly.
options.why: A database outage would restart every pod and lengthen recovery.

options.text: In both endpoints with a generous 30 second timeout inside each, to be thorough about it.
options.why: Slow dependency calls in liveness only make the restart storm worse.

options.text: In `/health/ready` only; `/health/live` just returns 200 if the process responds.
options.why: Correct: readiness failure removes the pod from traffic without killing it.

options.text: In neither endpoint; health routes must never call anything outside the process.
options.why: Readiness checks on critical dependencies are standard.

questions.explanation: Keep both routes cheap and time-boxed (`asyncio.wait_for` around the ping) and let the orchestrator decide using readiness for traffic and liveness for deadlocks.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which are sound practices for configuration and secrets in a FastAPI service?

options.text: Inject passwords through environment variables or a secrets manager.
options.why: Keeps secrets out of the repository and the image.

options.text: Commit a `.env` file that contains production credentials.
options.why: Anything in version-control history must be treated as compromised.

options.text: Use `SecretStr` in pydantic settings so values are masked in `repr` and logs.
options.why: `get_secret_value()` is required to read the real value.

options.text: Print `settings.model_dump()` at startup to help debugging.
options.why: That writes secret values into log aggregation.

options.text: Let `BaseSettings` fail at startup when a required variable is missing.
options.why: A crash at boot is cheaper than a failure on the first request.

options.text: Bake the API key into the Docker image.
options.why: Anyone who can pull the image can read the key.

questions.explanation: Principle: config in the environment (twelve-factor), secrets from a vault, validate at boot, never log them.

questions.prompt: True or false: with `acks_late=True` a Celery message is acknowledged only after the task finishes, so a worker crash mid-task leads to redelivery.

options.why: Correct: the broker still holds the unacknowledged message and hands it to another worker.
Wrong: late acknowledgement keeps the message on the broker until the task finishes, so a crash causes redelivery.

questions.explanation: This is why tasks must be idempotent. The default (early ack) risks losing a task on a crash instead.

questions.prompt: True or false: it is good practice to pass a full ORM object as an argument to a Celery task.

options.why: Wrong: serialising entities is fragile and the data may be stale by the time the task runs.
Correct: pass identifiers or small plain values and re-load inside the task, so it sees fresh data and the message stays small.

questions.explanation: Task arguments must be serialisable (JSON by default). A stale object also hides the "row was deleted meanwhile" case.
